Collared scops owls (Otus lettia) hatch from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with the altricial nestlings emerging after an incubation period that typically lasts 25 days [ab = 25 days]. The initial wet weight of these newly hatched chicks is remarkably modest, averaging just 14.2 grams [Ww0 = 14.2 grams], which represents only about ten percent of the mass they will eventually attain as adults. This lightweight beginning is typical of many small-bodied owl species, where the energetic demands of producing a calcareous egg constrain the resources that can be allocated to the yolk, resulting in a relatively underdeveloped nestling at the moment of hatching. The subsequent growth trajectory is rapid, fueled by the intensive biparental provisioning that begins almost immediately after the first feeding event.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is pronounced in this species, with adult females reaching a substantially larger ultimate wet weight. Field surveys and captive records indicate that the maximum adult body mass attained by females is 142 grams [Wwi = 142 grams], whereas males achieve a more modest adult mass of 112 grams [Wwi = 112 grams]. This degree of reversed sexual size dimorphism, where the female is the larger sex, is a well-documented pattern among strigid owls and has been linked to several functional hypotheses, including the energetic demands of egg production and the need for females to defend the nest and young against potential predators. The 30 gram difference between the sexes represents a roughly 27 percent greater mass in females, a disparity that places Otus lettia within the typical range observed for its genus.

Under the stable thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic period of the Collared scops owl, maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], several key developmental and reproductive milestones have been documented. The maximum lifespan recorded in wild individuals is approximately 3,212 days [am = approximately 3,212 days], which equates to slightly more than 8.8 years and reflects the relatively slow life-history pace typical of small owls at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation in these cavity-nesting birds, is reached at 157.5 days after hatching [tp = 157.5 days after hatching], indicating that somatic growth is largely completed within the first five to six months of life at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity is consistent with the species' occupation of productive, low-altitude forest habitats where seasonal food availability is generally reliable.

Also measured under those same thermoneutral conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the basal oxygen consumption rate of the Collared scops owl has been determined via open-flow respirometry to be 102.41 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 102.41 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This basal metabolic rate is indicative of the species' moderate energetic demands and falls within the expected range for a bird of its mass, particularly given the relatively low activity levels associated with its sit-and-wait foraging strategy. Fledging, marking the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest cavity, occurs at 52.5 days after hatching [tx = 52.5 days after hatching], though the literature also cites a broader developmental window of 18 to 26 days for the actual fledging process at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The extended time to fledging reflects the altricial nature of the nestlings, which require a prolonged period under parental care to grow their flight feathers and develop the neuromuscular coordination necessary for nocturnal hunting.

The reproductive output of the Collared scops owl is constrained by a single annual breeding attempt. Females typically lay 3 to 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 5 eggs per clutch], and the species produces only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year]. Under the prevailing thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the first successful brood is produced at 401.5 days since birth [tR = 401.5 days since birth], a figure that corresponds to approximately 1.1 years of age and aligns closely with the onset of sexual maturity documented earlier. The narrow reproductive window is further constrained by the relatively small clutch size and the extended period of parental care, which together limit the species' annual recruitment potential. Comparative studies within the genus Otus suggest that this conservative reproductive strategy is an adaptation to the stochastic prey availability that characterizes many forest ecosystems, where the energetic cost of rearing even a single brood is substantial.
